judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1187, which limits when a sewer authority can take a person's home over unpaid sewer bills. When a sewer bill goes unpaid, a town or regional authority can put a legal claim, called a lien, on the property. It can then force a sale of the home to collect. It can also sell that claim to a private buyer, who can force the sale. The new law protects homes the owner lives in. For those homes, the authority can act only if the unpaid amount is more than $3,000. It can also act once the bill has gone unpaid for three years. The limit does not apply when the sewer claim is handled together with unpaid property taxes or other town claims. It passed the Connecticut House of Representatives 84-65 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1221, which expands Connecticut's state-run retirement savings program. The program gives private-sector workers a retirement account when their employer does not offer one. Starting July 1, 2026, it also covers home care aides. They must be paid through a state-funded program, such as the Connecticut Home Care Program for Elders. Workers who join on or after July 1, 2025 get a new default savings rate. It is tied to a federal rule on minimum savings rates in private plans. The law also changes how the state enforces the rules against employers. Those rules cover employers who fail to sign workers up, or who send the money in late. Some lower-income savers get a matching payment from the federal government. The program's usual accounts cannot accept it, so the comptroller must offer an account that can. It passed the Connecticut House of Representatives 102-38 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1312, which changes several unemployment and workplace rules. Employers now have 40 days instead of 60 to protest a quarterly statement from the state. The protest covers benefits the state says were paid out by mistake or by fraud. The advocate who helps unemployed workers becomes a permanent state job. It used to be a job the labor commissioner could end at any time. Doctors, physician assistants and nurse practitioners get a new duty. They must tell the Labor Department within 48 hours if they think a patient's illness came from their job. The Shared Work program lets a company cut hours instead of laying people off. Employers used to avoid being charged for those benefits when statewide unemployment was high. Now they are charged. It passed the Connecticut House of Representatives 96-42 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1367, which bars bail bond agents from seizing someone at a hospital, a school or a house of worship. These agents track down people who were released on bail and did not come back to court. The ban covers the buildings, grounds and campus of these places. They are any state-run or state-licensed health care facility, the office of a licensed health care provider, any school or college, and any house of worship. When someone skips court, the bond agent owes the bail money. A judge can now cancel that penalty if the person is at one of those health care places. The judge also releases the agent and the insurance company. Before, a judge could generally only do that if the person was locked up in another state, with proof of it. Prosecutors also had to decline to bring the person back. It passed the Connecticut House of Representatives 93-55 and became law.
